summary: Sugilite is a rare, vivid purple stone of South Africa and Japan, called the love stone of the Aquarian age. Explore its meaning, care and look-alikes.
intro: Sugilite is a deep purple to magenta stone with a velvety, almost jelly-like glow when cut. The best material, from the Wessels Mine in South Africa, is a rich royal purple and highly translucent, and it commands high prices as a gem. It is usually sold as cabochons, beads or carvings, and is often streaked with black manganese or brown patches. The colour is a powerful violet that seems to hum on the skin. Because supply is limited and quality varies enormously, sugilite is a stone where grade truly matters, and lesser pieces are often dyed or mixed with other minerals.
history: Sugilite was first found in 1944 by the Japanese petrologist Ken-ichi Sugi on Iwagi Island, and named for him after it was formally described in 1976. For years it was a scientific curiosity until bright purple gem-quality material was found in the Wessels Mine in the Kalahari manganese field of South Africa in the 1970s. The vivid stone was briefly nicknamed luvulite and sold as a gem. It quickly became a favourite in the New Age movement, which called it the love stone for the new age of Aquarius, a status it has kept despite its rarity.
meaning: Sugilite is regarded as a stone of spiritual love and purpose. Its rich purple is linked to the crown and third eye, and also, in some traditions, to the heart. Practitioners use it to encourage acceptance of difference, to ease the feeling of not belonging, and to help discern what you truly came here to do. It is associated with spiritual protection and with a loving, universal attitude. Many people turn to it in times of questioning or transition, hoping for guidance from higher intuition. It is a stone sometimes chosen by those who feel highly sensitive, as it is said to help balance emotional openness with strength.
howToUse: Hold a piece of sugilite during meditation or prayer, focusing on the crown and breathing gently. Wear it as a pendant or ring when you want a reminder of your spiritual path and self-acceptance. Place it on a bedside table or altar as a symbol of love and wisdom. For a sense of calm after emotional stress, hold it for a few minutes while focusing on slow breathing. In grids, combine it with amethyst and clear quartz. Wear it for short periods, as some find it quite intense.
care: Sugilite is moderately hard and generally robust, and a quick rinse in lukewarm water is fine, but avoid long soaks and harsh chemicals. Dry it with a soft cloth. Cleanse by smoke, sound or selenite, and charge in moonlight. Strong sunlight can fade its purple, so keep it out of long direct sun. Store separately in a pouch so that harder stones do not scratch it. Avoid inhaling dust when cutting or polishing, as it may contain manganese.
identify: Fine sugilite is deep, even purple with a waxy to glassy translucence, often with black or brown patches of manganese oxide. Cheap beads sold as sugilite are frequently dyed howlite, dyed jade, charoite or purple glass. Genuine gem-grade material is rare and expensive, so be sceptical of bargains. Low-grade material is often stabilised or bonded with resin. Look for natural variation in colour and a heavy, dense feel. Ask the seller about origin and treatments, as South African material is the standard.

faq.a: In crystal tradition, sugilite is a stone of spiritual love, purpose and acceptance, linked to the crown and third eye. People use it for meditation and protection. These are metaphysical beliefs, not medical claims.

Gem-quality sugilite is very rare and comes mainly from the Wessels Mine in South Africa. Fine, evenly coloured, translucent purple pieces are scarce, while most material is low-grade, which is why top quality commands high prices.
A brief rinse in lukewarm water is usually fine, but avoid prolonged soaking and chemicals. Dry it well. Many people prefer smoke, sound or selenite for cleansing to protect the polish.
